title: Trump’s Iran War: Power to the People
author: Bill Scheuerman
content:
Months in, Trump’s war on Iran has netted him none of the goals he proclaimed
when he began dropping bombs. Iran still has a dictatorship, enriched uranium,
plenty of missiles and drones, and effective control of the now-closed Strait
of Hormuz. Military observers repeatedly tell the press that for Trump to
seize control of the Strait and Iran’s uranium would require a U.S. military
invasion, “boots on the ground.” So, what’s stopping him? Obviously, it’s not
the Constitution, which gives the power to declare war to Congress, not the
President. And it’s not the Republican controlled Congress, which is too
spineless to check Trump’s actions. So, again, what’s stopping Trump? Law and
rules mean nothing to him. Maybe Trump has given the answer himself: “My own
mind. It's the only thing that can stop me.”

Maybe what’s on Trump’s mind is a wary and discontented public. A recent Ipsos
poll found that more than 2/3 of Americans oppose his war. The war is not an
abstraction. It’s hitting Americans where it hurts the most – in their
pocketbooks. A recent NBC News report claimed that the war has cost U.S.
households more than $1,200 each thanks to rising gas and grocery prices. The
war is so unpopular that even 20% of MAGA voters oppose it, according to
POLITICO. Trump’s overall approval numbers are in free fall. The Economist
reports that as of a few days ago, Trump’s net approval has dropped a whopping
23 points since his reelection. Sixty percent of Americans disapprove of his
performance. So far that public disapproval hasn’t changed his course of
action on much of anything. But if Trump were to authorize a ground invasion
of Iran, public opinion may quickly turn into an active bipartisan movement in
the streets to end Trump’s war, and effectively, his presidency.

Trump may well be mindful of a lot of history here. Since the end of World War
II, a series of failed wars has brought down presidents. Korea ended Harry
Truman’s presidency just as Vietnam killed the presidencies of Lyndon Johnson
and Richard Nixon. Ronald Reagan’s Iran-Contra debacle brought him to the
precipice of impeachment. Trump grew up watching presidencies get chewed up in
American military failures. He is old enough to remember how young people
fought to end a war in Vietnam that he avoided with “bone spurs.” He knows
that Richard Nixon’s impatience with that protest helped to bring on the
Watergate scandal that ended his presidency. He knows equally well that the
futility of America’s interminable bloody wars in Afghanistan and Iraq badly
deflated George W. Bush’s presidential power and made him a candidate for
worst president in American history. Trump knows that more is at stake here
than Republican control of Congress. Viscerally, he senses that the fate of
his personal power, which is to say, his very idea of himself as America’s
monarch, as King Donald, hinges on popular docility. In June, he lamented to
Fox News that he doubted that “America has the stomach” for the ground-level
war required to achieve his objectives.

The idea of “boots on the ground” is the bloody red line of democracy that
even King Donald fears to cross. There is an important lesson here. Much has
been justifiably written about Trump’s violation of informal democratic norms
and constitutional rules. He has in countless ways tossed the institutions of
procedural democracy into the garbage heap of his presidency. But it is
important to remember that democracy is not only about norms and procedures.
It is about ordinary people working in concert not only to voice but to affirm
and take direct action. Millions have already done so in thousands of No Kings
demonstrations. But those protests, as important as they have been, only hint
at the democratic fury and power that Trump would unleash in a ground invasion
of Iran. Democracy is not just a matter of procedures, institutions and norms.
At the heart of authentic democracy is what economist Mehrdad Vahabi calls the
people’s “scream power.” Democratic “scream power” ended the rule of earlier
war presidents. King Donald, we think, grasps this elemental fact. Democracy
scares him. This is no time to let up the pressure.
